AI-and-Work/Where-the-Work-Goes.title: Where the Work Goes
AI-and-Work/Where-the-Work-Goes.content:
If AI can’t end scarcity, it moves it. Two spectrums for guessing where.

In Why the Age of Abundance Won’t Feel Like One I argued that AI can end a lot of scarcity, but not wanting. If that’s right, work isn’t going away. It’s moving, the way it always has.
“Computer” used to be a job title. Rooms of people did calculations by hand, all day. Machines took that work, and the people moved on to other work. Nobody today misses being a human calculator.
So the interesting question isn’t whether work survives AI. It’s where it goes. I use two spectrums to think about that. Neither is a prediction. They’re more like a compass.
First, where the leftover scarcity lives
Once food, shelter and health are taken care of, what’s left is mostly the positional economy: wanting to stand out from the people around you. A better car than your neighbour’s, a nicer wedding than your cousin’s, more respect in your office.
This kind of scarcity isn’t limited by resources. It’s limited by people. The anthropologist Robin Dunbar found that across primates, the size of the social group tracks the size of the neocortex. For humans that works out to roughly 150 people we can keep real relationships with. That’s the circle you compare yourself to.
That circle doesn’t grow when factories get faster. You will always be part of a small group, and you’ll always measure yourself against it. Production can flood the world with stuff. It can’t flood the thing that’s actually scarce, which is standing out within your circle.
Keep that in mind, because both spectrums lead back to it.
Spectrum one: from utility to art


ART
UTILITY

← technology keeps pushing things this way
WATCHES




keeps time
says who you are
PAINTING




looks real
means something


New technology starts out competing on usefulness. A faster phone, a waterproof watch: pay more and you get more. Even status is tied to utility at this stage. The rich have the better thing because it is better.
Then technology makes the useful thing so cheap that everyone has it. The utility race is over, but the wish to be different from everyone else isn’t. So scarcity gets brought back artificially, through brand, craft, design, limited editions, and sometimes just the price itself.
Watches are the clearest case. Cheap, perfectly accurate watches arrived decades ago, and now your phone tells the time anyway. Telling time is basically free. The watch market didn’t die. It moved to the far left of this spectrum, where a watch is mostly a statement about who you are. You can watch the same thing happen with clothes, where cheap and decent became the norm and logos took over, and with phones, where nearly every phone is good enough and which one you carry still says something.
Art moves too
You might think art is the next thing AI takes over. But art itself has always followed this pattern.
Before cameras, a lot of painting was valued for accuracy: a portrait that really looked like the person, a landscape that looked like the place. Then photography made accurate images abundant. The craving for beauty didn’t go away. Its target moved, toward impressions, abstraction, and eventually modern art with its strange lines and shapes. Duchamp once put a signed urinal in an exhibition and called it art. I honestly can’t tell you why it’s art, and that’s my point. Art moved to where the scarcity was: novelty, a message, a context, culture, sometimes politics. Being different became part of what makes something art.
So when AI can make any image in any style on demand, art doesn’t end. It moves again, toward what instant abundance can’t supply: a particular person, a story, a context, a reason it exists.
Not just old things with an art sticker
I don’t mean the future economy is today’s products with a luxury label on them. A lot of existing things will go that way, but there will also be new kinds of goods, and they’re hard to imagine in advance.
Handicraft is a good example from the past. Once machines made goods cheap, handmade things became more valuable, not less. They carry cultural context, and they’re scarce because human hands are scarce.
People already complain that modern buildings are bland and lifeless next to the colourful, ornate buildings of the past. That complaint is the same pattern again: we look for novelty wherever scarcity still exists.
Or take a stranger one. If one day everyone has an AI companion, a human partner might become a status symbol. Some people might even put up with a difficult relationship partly because of what it signals. I don’t know if that will happen. I’m less interested in guessing the products than in the desire underneath them, which doesn’t change: to be seen, and to be different.
Spectrum two: from tech to product to sales
This one sounds corporate, but it isn’t. Look at almost any system that involves people and you’ll find the same layers.



Sales
being seen, trust, relationships

Product
what to build, who does what

Tech
building it: the bricks
AI is taking over this layer



move up, not sideways


At the bottom is implementation: the real building blocks. Bricks for a house, code for software, hands and labour for most things.
Above that is product: deciding what to build, and coordinating the people building it.
At the top is the part that makes the system visible to the world: selling it, building trust, keeping relationships alive. The social side of a system sits at the top because coordinating people and reaching people is what the lower layers exist to serve.
A household, a temple, a startup and a government all have these layers. So this isn’t really about companies. It describes any system with people in it, which is nearly all of them.
The bottom layer has always run away
Technology has been eating parts of the bottom layer forever. Each time, the people doing that work ran sideways into a different kind of implementation. Human calculators became programmers. Farm workers moved into factories, and factory workers into offices. It never happened that every kind of implementation was taken at once, so there was always somewhere sideways to go.
That’s what’s different now. AI isn’t taking one kind of implementation. It’s coming for the layer.
People say physical work like welding and plumbing will be safe for a long time. Maybe. But given the pace of robotics and energy, I’m not betting on it. I also don’t need to, because the bottom isn’t the only place people work. Every layer of a system has people in it. So don’t run sideways. Run up.
Can AI take the top too?
The obvious reply is that AI will do sales as well. Sales bots will flood every inbox.
They probably will. But the top layer runs into the same limit as the positional economy: human attention. People can only keep up so many relationships. That’s Dunbar again. A lot of what happens at the top is like a keep-alive signal: staying in touch, showing up, slowly earning trust, being someone people actually know. AI has no motives of its own. It always acts on someone’s behalf. A flood of bots doesn’t increase the number of people anyone can hold in their head. If anything it makes the few slots in that head more valuable.
Which raises the question: if everything is abundant, what’s being sold up there? The answer goes back to spectrum one. It’s whatever the scarcity has moved to: craft, art, culture, status, and human attention itself.
What I do about it
So what if my job is the kind that’s likely to disappear?
I use the two spectrums to decide what to get better at. On both of them, I move left: toward art and the human side, and up toward the social layer. I’m an introvert, and I’m deliberately working on the social side anyway: psychology, communication, networking, art, culture. As the non-human work gets automated, being more human becomes the valuable part.
Learn in a language that travels
The other thing I do is about how I learn. I’ll write about this properly another time, but here’s the short version.
If you store what you learn in the vocabulary of one system, like physics formulas or the syntax of one programming language, it stays in that system. If you store it in a more abstract language, it travels.
Abstract algebra is the best example I know. It doesn’t study numbers, or shapes, or matrices. It studies a group: any set of things with a way of combining them, as long as four simple rules hold. Combining two things gives you something still in the set. The order in which you group the combinations doesn’t matter. There’s one element that changes nothing. Every action can be undone. Prove a theorem about groups once, and it holds at the same time for clock arithmetic, for rotating a square, for matrices, and for the moves on a Rubik’s cube.











one abstract
pattern

Physics
Code
Philosophy
People
Product
Sales



There’s a catch. The abstraction must not strip away the usefulness. If you drop any of those four rules, you can prove almost nothing interesting. Too abstract and you know nothing; too concrete and you know one thing. The skill is finding the right level.
When you find it, things start connecting. A lesson from physics shows up in philosophy. What a relationship teaches you about people turns into empathy you can use in product or sales.
That isn’t a coincidence. Every one of those domains runs on the same substrate: the same kind of brain, with a small set of desires and well-understood ways of acting on them. The patterns repeat because the thing producing them is the same.

AI will take a lot of work, and the scarcity will move to where the humans are: standing out, making things that mean something, being trusted by a few people who know you. So move up, move toward the human, and learn in a way that travels.

AI-and-Work/Why-the-Age-of-Abundance-Won.title: Why the Age of Abundance Won't Feel Like One
AI-and-Work/Why-the-Age-of-Abundance-Won.content:
AI can end a lot of scarcity. It can’t end wanting.

You’ve probably heard some version of this: AI is going to take your job, but don’t worry. An age of abundance is coming, everything will be cheap, and work will be optional.
Every time I hear it, something in me pushes back. It’s not that I doubt the technology. I doubt the part about us.
You already know how this goes
Think of something you badly wanted a few years ago: a job, a salary, a phone, a house, a person’s approval. Maybe you got it. How long did it feel like enough?
Not long, probably. The new thing became normal, and a new want took its place. Nobody has to explain this to you; you’ve lived it. It’s why people keep telling each other to practise gratitude and be content with what they have. A restless mind doesn’t stop on its own.
Now look at the richest countries in the world. By the standards of almost any earlier century, they already live in an age of abundance: food everywhere, comfort everywhere, entertainment without end. They also have a huge amount of depression, anxiety and dissatisfaction. Abundance arrived there, and the feeling of abundance didn’t come with it.
The sentence the treadmill always says
There’s a particular sentence your mind keeps telling you: once this is done, everything will be sorted. Once I get the job. Once I clear the loan. Once I move out. Then I’ll be at peace.
“Once AI makes everything abundant, we’ll be free” is the same sentence, said for a whole civilisation. It looks at the scarcity we have today, imagines it gone, and assumes nothing takes its place. That’s exactly the mistake the treadmill makes in each of us.
Two kinds of scarcity
I want to be fair here, because some scarcity is very real.
Some of it is imposed from outside. People are stuck in wars. People don’t have enough to eat. People have diseases that can’t be cured, or can be cured but they can’t afford it. AI may well shrink this kind of scarcity enormously, and that would be one of the best things ever to happen to humanity. I’m not dismissing it.
Some of it is made inside: wanting more than the people around you, wanting the next level, wanting to matter. No amount of production fills it, because it’s measured against other people, or against a version of yourself that keeps moving.
The bucket
Here’s how I picture it. Your scarcity is a bucket full of demands. Some came from outside: food, safety, health. Some you made yourself.
When AI removes the outside demands, the bucket doesn’t empty. The space gets filled with demands of the second kind. It doesn’t happen because something went wrong. It’s how we work: the mind always finds the next thing to want.
So my first claim is simple. AI will change what we want, not how much we want.
Is the new suffering smaller?
The natural reply is: fine, people will still want things, but suffering over status is nothing like suffering from hunger. Surely the world gets better on average.
At face value that’s obviously right, and at the extremes it is right. I’d still push on it a little, in the other direction.
First, pain is pain. The brain doesn’t keep separate books for “real” suffering and “mental” suffering. Think of someone who is depressed despite having everything. Their pain doesn’t feel less real to them because they have a nice apartment. I’m not sure we get to call it smaller.
Second, people adapt to hardship far more than it looks from outside. From the outside, poverty looks like hell. From the inside, life there often looks surprisingly familiar. People compete with each other, celebrate small wins over their neighbours, get used to physical hardship, and get excited about simple things. A rich person gets a thrill from a Lamborghini. A poor person can get the same thrill from a new bicycle. Measured as an experience, those two thrills may be closer than we think.
I can’t measure any of this, and I’m not claiming the two kinds of suffering are equal. I’m saying the gap is probably smaller than it looks, and that adaptation works in both directions. We get used to having more, and we also get used to having less.
So what do we do with this?
None of this is an argument against AI, or against ending hunger and disease. Do all of it, as fast as possible.
It’s an argument against waiting. If the age of abundance won’t feel like abundance, there’s no point postponing contentment until it arrives. The bucket was never going to be emptied from outside. Whatever peace we get, we’ll have to find it inside, now, with whatever we have. That’s the one thing no machine can do for us.
If that idea interests you, it’s what Microframeworks is about: can you be at peace first, and then do the thing?

Mind/Heart-or-Mind-Is-the-Wrong-Question.title: Heart or Mind Is the Wrong Question
Mind/Heart-or-Mind-Is-the-Wrong-Question.content:
What people mean when they say “my heart told me”, and a better question to ask instead

“Listen to your heart.” “Use your head.” You’ve probably heard both, maybe about the same decision. We talk as if there are two advisers inside us: a warm, intuitive one in the chest and a cold, calculating one in the skull. And when people tell the stories of the big choices in their lives, the heart usually wins.
But try to say what the heart actually is. Not the organ, the voice. What makes a thought count as coming from the heart rather than the mind? I’ve never heard a clear answer. When you look closely, the split falls apart, and what’s left is more useful.
When do we say “heart”?
Take a few situations.
Someone finds a way to make a lot of money, but it means cutting two colleagues out of a deal. Part of them says, “do it, it’s a lot of money”. Another part says, “that’s wrong”. We’d call the first one the mind, the greedy, scheming mind, and the second one the heart.
Someone has a stable job. Every sensible argument says stay. But something keeps telling them to leave and try the thing they actually care about. They leave, it works out, and years later they say, “my heart told me to go”.
Someone falls for a person who is obviously a risk. The mind says be careful. The heart says go for it.
Look at what the heart is doing in each case. In the first, it’s the moral voice. In the second, it’s the brave one. In the third, it’s the voice of desire, and the mind is the cautious, scared one. The heart isn’t consistently rational or irrational, careful or bold, selfless or selfish. It changes sides.



MIND
HEART
MONEY
cut them out
greed
that's wrong
morals
JOB
stay, it's safe
caution
leave
courage
LOVE
too risky
fear
go for it
desire
the side we admire


What the heart’s voice has in common
Two things, as far as I can tell.
First, the heart usually doesn’t come with a reason. “I want the money, and here’s how I get it” is an argument you can lay out step by step. “That’s wrong” mostly isn’t, and neither is “something told me to leave”. When people can’t say why they feel something, they tend to say it came from the heart.
Second, the heart gets the motives that sound good out loud: empathy, guilt, conscience, loyalty, love, courage, faith. The mind gets the ones you’d rather keep quiet about: greed, ambition, lust, the fear of looking foolish. Roughly, if it’s safe to say at a dinner table, it goes to the heart.
These two go together for a reason. The motives we admire are mostly feelings, not arguments. You don’t reason your way into feeling guilty. You just do.
It’s all one brain
Here’s what I think is actually going on. There’s no second organ doing the thinking. There’s one brain, built by evolution, and evolution doesn’t care about our happiness or how we see ourselves. It only “cares” about what survives and reproduces.
For an animal living alone, pure self-interest might be enough. We don’t live alone. We’re social animals, and a member of the group who only ever grabs for themselves gets pushed out, and on their own they don’t last long. So evolution gave us two sets of instincts: one that looks after me, and one that looks after us. Hunger, greed and ambition on one side. Guilt, empathy, loyalty and shame on the other.
Both are impulses. Both arrive without asking permission, and both can be completely unreasonable. The guilt you feel after snapping at a waiter is just as automatic as the craving for a third slice of cake.
What we call heart and mind is how we sort these impulses when we talk about them. The ones that serve the group, we admire, so they get the noble name. The ones that serve ourselves, we’re a little embarrassed by, so we pin them on the calculating mind, even when there’s nothing calculated about them.
Why the heart got the job
You can feel your heart race when you’re scared or in love. The feelings seem to happen in your chest, so for most of history people assumed that’s where they came from. The ancient Egyptians thought the heart was where thinking happened: when they mummified someone, they kept the heart and threw the brain away. Aristotle thought the brain’s job was to cool the blood.
Science moved thinking into the head a long time ago, but the language never caught up. The heart kept all the romance.
The question to ask instead
If “heart” and “mind” are labels we paste on afterwards, then “should I follow my heart or my mind?” isn’t a real choice. Either voice can be right, and either can be shallow.
Greed can be shallow: money now, without seeing what it costs you with the people around you. Conscience can be shallow too: guilt over something that hurts nobody. And the job that “my heart told me” to leave worked out, but we rarely hear from the many people whose heart said the same thing and it didn’t.
The better question is: how deep does this argument go? Can I follow it a few steps further? What does this voice want, and what happens after I get it? Take any voice, heart or mind, and ask it to explain itself. Some will hold up when you push. Some won’t.
That’s the thread I want to pull next. I think a lot of people sabotage themselves, not by listening to the wrong voice, but by following a shallow argument from either one without noticing.

Mind/How-You-Sabotage-Yourself-Without-K.title: How You Sabotage Yourself Without Knowing It
Mind/How-You-Sabotage-Yourself-Without-K.content:
Three traps the mind sets for you, why they’re so hard to see, and how to step out of them

Self-sabotage comes in two kinds. In the first, you know exactly what you’re doing. You know the third drink is a bad idea and you have it anyway. That’s a problem of self-control, and it isn’t what this piece is about.
The second kind is harder, because you don’t know you’re doing it. You’re stuck, and the story you tell yourself about why sounds completely reasonable. This piece is about that kind.
In The War Between You and Your Mind I described how evolution built a mind whose priorities aren’t yours. Here I want to look at a few specific places where those priorities set traps: loops that keep a person suffering, and that feel, from the inside, like simply who they are.


                  
                  What this article is not saying 
                  
                

Depression, anxiety and insomnia are real. Biology may well be the main driver of them: genes, brain chemistry, physical health. They deserve real treatment.
This article is about another factor that sits on top: psychological traps. These can affect anyone, including people with no biological predisposition at all, and they can make a real condition harder to escape.
It’s never one cause. The question isn’t whether a trap is involved (some version of it is involved for everyone) but how much of what keeps you stuck is the trap.


The mind can make you sad, if sadness pays
Start with the part that sounds wrong. Why would your own mind make you sad?
Because sadness can be rewarded. You’ve probably felt this. You’re upset and alone, and you’re holding it together. Then someone sits down next to you and asks if you’re okay, and suddenly it gets worse. Your eyes fill up, and you’re crying in a way you weren’t a minute ago.
Nobody plans that, and nobody’s faking. It’s an old, evolved response: for a social animal, showing distress to someone who cares gets you help. But it shows that the mind can produce sadness when sadness earns something. Psychologists have a name for that payoff: secondary gain, the attention, care or relief a symptom brings with it.
And anything that pays can become a loop. Once a state earns a reward, the mind keeps steering you back into it. Over time it starts to look a lot like addiction: a pleasure that’s bad for you, and hard to put down.
Trap one: the tortured genius
Everyone wants to feel special, and almost everyone wants to feel smart.
There’s a hard way to get that: make something that actually helps people, and let the value show. And there’s an easier way: become the tortured genius. Be visibly troubled. Talk like someone who sees through everything.
You’ve seen the posts. “The curse of knowing too much.” “Ignorance is bliss.” “Happy people just don’t think enough.” “Too smart to be happy.” The message is the same every time: my suffering is proof of my depth.
That message pays. It earns validation from other people, and from yourself. And it strokes the ego from an unexpected direction: I’m sad because I understand. Look at all those dumb, happy people.
This doesn’t mean everyone who talks like this is a fraud. It isn’t black and white. Someone in this trap may really be sharp, and that sensitivity may be exactly what made them prone to it. But being genuine doesn’t make you immune to the mechanism, any more than being a monk stops your brain reacting to weed. The question isn’t whether the person is real. It’s how much of what keeps them stuck is the reward.
(And it isn’t a claim about whether intelligence and mental illness are linked. Maybe they are. That’s a different question.)
Trap two: trauma as a badge
The worst thing about trauma isn’t always the trauma itself. It’s what the trauma becomes afterwards: a ready-made excuse that later traps can lean on. The mind is lazy, and it will use whatever leverage it can find.
I’m not writing this from outside. I grew up in my uncle’s house while my mother lived with schizophrenia, and I lost her slowly, over months. I came out of it with social anxiety, trust issues and trouble sleeping, and every one of them offered me a badge to wear.
Anyone who’s been through something hard reaches a fork. You can fight what it did to you, or you can wear it.
Take someone who grew up feeling like a burden in the house they lived in. They learn to make themselves invisible, and by adulthood it has become social anxiety: every room feels like a place where they’ll be noticed and not wanted. They can work at it, slowly and painfully. Or they can say “I’m like this because of how I grew up”, and stop there.
Once you start looking, the badges are everywhere. “I have daddy issues.” “I grew up in an abusive household, so of course I do drugs.” “My parents divorced, so I don’t do relationships.” “I have trust issues.” “Nobody really wants to talk to me anyway.”
Here’s the uncomfortable part. A healed, ordinary life doesn’t come with a story. If you get better, there’s nothing to explain. If you keep sabotaging your relationships, you get to say “I come from a toxic childhood, so I can’t get close to people”, and that one sentence carries an identity and sympathy at the same time. Nobody decides this consciously. The mind just never steers you towards getting better, because staying where you are keeps paying.
Labels stack traps
The most dangerous labels are the ones that pay in several ways at once.
Say your mother had insomnia, and you have trouble sleeping too. Some of that may well be real. Now it’s two in the morning and your mind wants the phone. “I have insomnia, like my mother” is the perfect excuse. And look at how much that one label feeds.




an excuse
the phone at 2 a.m.

sympathy
when you mention it

ONE LABEL
"I have insomnia"

a story
"like my mother"

an identity
can't switch off


The excuse to keep scrolling. The sympathy when you mention it. The trauma story. Even the tortured-genius identity, the one who can’t switch off. One label, four payoffs. That’s why some labels are so hard to put down: you’d be giving up four rewards at once.
Trap three: buying certainty
This last trap is quieter, and it doesn’t need anyone else to be watching.
If you’ve played badminton or table tennis, you may have noticed something odd: people often start falling apart just when they’re winning. A run of easy points, then suddenly a string of unforced errors. Here’s what I think is going on. A close, winning game is intense. You have to focus, you’re anxious, and you have to live with not knowing how it ends. Then you throw a few points, and the uncertainty is gone. You’re losing. That’s bad, but at least it’s settled.
The same thing happens off the court. You’re waiting on a result that comes out tomorrow, you have a chance to find out today, and you take it, even when knowing early only makes things worse. The answer isn’t the point. The point is to stop not knowing.
Ideas get the same treatment. You get an idea that could turn into something good, and almost immediately your mind finds a reason to drop it. It’s been done. It won’t work. You don’t have time. Sometimes those reasons are right. But often what’s really being avoided is the months of hard, uncertain work the idea would ask for. “It probably wouldn’t have worked anyway” ends the uncertainty tonight.
The visible version of this is familiar: you know the answer in class and still can’t raise your hand. You know you’re scared, so that one isn’t hidden. The hidden versions are the ones above, where the fear dresses up as a sensible reason.
The pattern underneath
All three traps share one root. The mind is an algorithm shaped by evolution, and it was never shaped for your well-being. It reaches for whatever pays right now: validation, sympathy, relief from uncertainty. It doesn’t check whether the payment ruins your next ten years.
And these traps are rarely all or nothing. Every behaviour has many causes. Your biology, your history and your circumstances all pull at once, and the trap is one more force on top of them. But it’s the one you can do something about most directly.
The way out
The answer is the same in every case: don’t take your thoughts and feelings at face value. Look at the motive behind them.
Name the payoff. When you catch yourself saying “I’m like this because…”, ask what that sentence gets you. Sympathy? A story? Permission not to try? Relief from not knowing? You don’t have to say it out loud. You just have to see it.
Follow the argument one more step. “I’m like this because of X, so I can’t” is a shallow argument. It stops exactly where it’s convenient. Ask: can’t, or haven’t yet? Does everyone with X end up like this? (In Heart or Mind Is the Wrong Question I argued that the real question is always how deep an argument goes.) Most of these fall apart at the second step.
Get the reward the hard way. The needs underneath are real: to feel special, to be cared for, to be close to people, to feel settled. The trap is only a cheap route to them. Make something and let it speak for you. Build closeness instead of being pitied into it. Practise sitting with uncertainty, a little longer each time.
Be patient with yourself. The loop has been paying you for years. It won’t vanish the moment you notice it, and the tools from The War Between You and Your Mind (meditation, patience, being soft on yourself) all apply here. But noticing is where it starts. A trap you can see is already half open.

Mind/The-Cost-of-Needing-to-Understand-E.content:
On bottom-up thinking, the bad memory that isn’t, and learning to trust the box

Some people can open a textbook the night before an exam, skim it, and walk out with good marks. If you’ve always envied them and never managed it yourself, see whether any of this sounds familiar:

You can’t learn a fact until you know why it’s true. Being told isn’t enough; you need to see it derived.
Subjects you can rebuild from a few principles come easily. Subjects that arrive as a pile of facts and exceptions feel impossible.
You’ve read the whole theory of something and never actually used it.
Your notes never get going, because you don’t understand the topic well enough to write them yet.
You look at an architecture diagram, a page of boxes and arrows, and nothing sticks.
Somewhere along the way, you decided you just have a bad memory.

I was like this for most of my life. I want to describe how it works, what it costs, and the odd moment it flipped, because I don’t think the problem is memory at all.
A good observation turned into a law
Somewhere around class eight, I made myself a rule. If I studied something, I’d understand it to the core. Otherwise it was a waste of time: I’d read it, forget it, and be left with nothing.
There was something true in that. Deep understanding is the kind that lasts, and the kind you can build on. The mistake was turning a useful observation into a law. Once it was a law, my mind simply refused to work with information it didn’t fully understand.
Call this bottom-up thinking. You start at the foundations and build upward, and you won’t stand on any floor until you’ve personally checked every floor below it. Top-down thinking goes the other way. You start with the big picture, accept its parts as given, and dig into the details only where you need to.
What bottom-up costs
The main cost is the price of entry. Before I could reason about even basic things in a subject, I had to build a deep, concrete model of how it worked.
In school this sorted subjects for me in a way I didn’t understand at the time. Geometry was easy because I could see it; algebra took much longer. Vectors were fine because I could picture arrows moving. Matrices and determinants were a grey zone, because I couldn’t picture what a determinant was. Chemistry was a disaster. It’s full of rules with exceptions, facts you’re expected to hold without deriving them, and I couldn’t hold them. I concluded that my memory was bad.
The same pattern followed me out of school. For years I wanted to get into machine learning. I read Michael Nielsen’s Neural Networks and Deep Learning and understood it down to the mathematics of how a network learns. I never trained a single model. For someone who thought the way I did, working in machine learning would have meant doing a PhD first, because I couldn’t act on anything I didn’t fully understand.
That’s the real shape of it. It isn’t laziness, and it isn’t a bad memory. It’s an inability to act under uncertainty.
The workarounds
Software made the problem impossible to ignore. Nobody can understand a modern software stack to the bottom; there’s far too much of it. The whole field runs on abstraction. You use things whose source you’ve never read, and you trust that they do what they say.
My mind wouldn’t do that, so I found a way around it. When I met a system I didn’t have time to learn properly, I’d invent a hypothetical version of it out of building blocks I already understood: things I’d seen working in real code, mechanisms I could picture end to end. How might the internet move a page from a server to my screen? How might a regex engine actually match a pattern? How might Git store history? For Kubernetes, I’d imagine how I would build it myself from parts I’d used before. The guesses didn’t have to be right. They only had to be made of real things, so that my mind would accept them.
This can sound like abstraction, but it’s the opposite. An abstraction asks you to accept a component by what it does, without knowing what it’s made of. My hypothetical models did the reverse. I couldn’t accept anything my mind couldn’t trace down to concrete parts, so when I didn’t have the real mechanism, I made up one that was plausible. It was still bottom-up thinking, just with invented foundations instead of real ones.
It worked, more or less, and it gave me a solid base for my job. Depth wasn’t useless either: in the few areas I understood well, it sometimes let me see an unusual way through. But every new system still needed its own homemade model before I could reason about it, and every one of them cost a lot to build. I was never going to be the person who learns it the night before.
The flip
The change came from somewhere unexpected: I was trying to work out how to organise my notes.
Note-taking had always been hard for me, and now I can see why. You take notes before you understand a subject, while it’s still half-formed. I couldn’t. My instinct was that my notes had to mirror reality. They were meant to document how things actually are, in my own words, so I could look at them later and recall the mechanics. You can’t mirror something you don’t understand yet, so I was stuck.
Then I thought about a biology textbook. If it mirrored reality, it would need a separate chapter for every human being, because that’s how we exist: billions of separate bodies with a lot in common. A textbook doesn’t do that. It describes one model body, organised into parts, and inside each part it describes the variants. The chapter on blood covers group A and group B, though no one has both. The book isn’t a copy of anyone. It’s a structure of its own, built so you can make sense of any real body you meet.
That was the realisation. Notes don’t mirror reality. They exist in their own right. An abstraction, a model, a box on a diagram is as real as anything made of atoms. It’s real in a different way, because its job is to help you move through reality rather than copy it. (It’s the same idea as in Logic Isn’t About Truth: a model has to be useful, not a replica.)
This probably comes naturally to a lot of people. For me it was a gift.
What changed
The first thing that changed was the architecture diagrams. I’d never really been able to look at Kubernetes, and the problem was never the diagram. It was that I didn’t respect the boxes. I didn’t believe in a component until I’d rebuilt it in my head from real parts. Once I accepted that the box is the thing, at least at that level, the diagrams started to stick.
Which suggests the “bad memory” was never about memory. There’s a well-known study from 1973. The psychologists William Chase and Herbert Simon showed chess positions to masters and beginners for a few seconds, then asked them to rebuild the board from memory. The masters did far better, but only on positions from real games. When the pieces were placed at random, the masters’ advantage mostly disappeared. They didn’t have better memories. They saw the board as chunks, meaningful patterns they already knew, and they remembered the chunks. Memory needs something to hang on. If your mind won’t accept the hooks, nothing sticks.
Other things followed:

I could take notes on half the picture, knowing I’d revise them.
I could start using something before I fully understood it, and let the use teach me.
I could act on less information, which is most of what people mean by high agency. Games like chess and poker may reward the same habit: you reason with patterns and odds, never with the whole picture.
I could work in a team. As a bottom-up thinker I couldn’t have worked with ten people, because nobody can understand everyone’s work to the bottom. You reason with the components other people built, and you trust their edges.

Now I build abstract components, treat them as real, and reason with them entirely inside the model. I no longer force each one back down to something physical first.
Why some subjects felt illogical
Looking back, chemistry wasn’t illogical, and neither are biology, finance or most of the things I avoided. These subjects work with partial information and real uncertainty. Chemistry has exceptions because the underlying physics is far too complicated to work out from scratch every time, so it gets summarised in rules that mostly hold. Financial models never fully describe a market. The people in these fields aren’t being sloppy. They’re doing the only thing anyone can when there’s more information than one person can hold: build high-level models, use them, and amend them as they learn.
If you’re a bottom-up thinker, the way in looks something like this:

Start from the top. Learn the main parts and how they connect before learning any one part in depth.
Treat the boxes as real. A component you don’t understand inside is still something you can reason with.
Go deeper only where the top fails. If the high-level model explains what you see, leave it. Dig into the one place where it doesn’t.
Expect to revise. A first model is meant to be replaced. It isn’t a promise.

That’s all it took: a change in what I counted as real. It came while I was organising my notes.

Mind/The-War-Between-You-and-Your-Mind.title: The War Between You and Your Mind
Mind/The-War-Between-You-and-Your-Mind.content:
Why the part of you that plans keeps losing to the part that craves, and why it might not be a war at all

You set an alarm for six to study before work. At six, something in you switches it off and goes back to sleep. You decide no phone after ten. At one in the morning you’re still scrolling.
So who decided, and who broke the decision? People have names for this: the higher self and the lower self, willpower and temptation, you and your mind. We use these words all the time and almost never say what they mean. I want to pin them down, look at why the two sides fight in the first place, and then suggest that the fight might be less serious than it feels.
Drawing the line
Here’s the simplest version I can give.
You, the self, is the part that plans. It can see far: next month, next year, the person you’d like to be in five years. It’s the part that set the alarm.
Your mind is everything else: cravings, moods, impulses, the quick reactions that fire before you’ve thought about anything. It sees only a short way ahead: this moment, tonight, maybe tomorrow. It’s the part that switched the alarm off. (What people call “the heart” belongs here too. I’ve argued in Heart or Mind Is the Wrong Question that it’s the same brain either way.)
This isn’t about being a monk. For most people the far-seeing self has ordinary goals: clear an exam, get fit, get a better job, save some money. The difference between the two sides isn’t what they want. It’s how far ahead they can see.
There’s one twist. The line between “me” and “my mind” isn’t fixed. It gets drawn by whichever part of you is doing the looking. At midnight, the part that wants one more episode feels like you. The next morning, looking back, it feels like something that happened to you. “I wasn’t myself.” Whatever we end up disapproving of gets moved to the other side of the line.


YOUR MIND
cravings, moods
YOU
plans, goals


now
years ahead

where "me" begins



and it moves


Why they fight
Your brain was built by evolution, and evolution is a blind process with one direction: survive and reproduce, then do it again. It handed us hunger for sugar and fat, fear of being left out, hunger for status, desire, the pull to grab what’s in front of us before someone else does.
None of this is there to torture you. These drives are the stepping stones that got us here. Without them, there’d be no animal clever enough to plan five years ahead in the first place.
But evolution only gave the whole thing a direction, and for evolution, direction was enough. It was never headed anywhere in particular. It just keeps going. The part of you that wants to arrive somewhere, to pass the exam, to be calm, to be healthy, was born along the way. It has different priorities from the forces that built it. And it can’t step outside them, because it lives in the same body and runs on the same brain.
That’s the war. Not good against evil, just two sets of priorities sharing one body.
Born on a sailboat
Here’s the picture I find most useful.
You were born on a sailboat in the open ocean. The wind is all those old drives. It was blowing long before you got here, and it doesn’t care where you want to go.
You can’t get off; there’s no shore you could survive on. You can’t stop the wind, and you don’t control it. You don’t get to choose whether you feel a craving, any more than a sailor gets to choose the weather. If you try to fight the wind head-on, you’ll wear yourself out and go nowhere.
But here’s the good part: the wind is also your only engine. A sailor doesn’t fight the wind; they trim the sails. They can even sail against the wind by zigzagging across it, which sailors call tacking. The same force that would blow you off course is the force that gets you home, if you learn to use it.


WIND
WIND


where you want to go


tacking:
using the wind




where the wind takes you


One more thing sailors know: a heavy boat turns slowly. You push the tiller and for a long while nothing seems to happen. Then the bow starts to come round.
What helps
Meditation. Strip away the mystique and meditation is practice at noticing a gust before it takes the boat. You sit, an urge shows up (check your phone, get up, think about that argument), and you watch it without doing what it says. Every time you do that, the urge loses a little of its grip, and the part of you that noticed gets a little stronger. It also starts to feel good, and whatever feels good, the brain does more of.
Patience, and being soft on yourself. You don’t control the wind, so you will lose some days. That isn’t failure; it’s weather. The boat turns slowly, so progress will be slow even when you’re doing everything right. Beating yourself up about it is just another gust, and it pushes the same way as the others: towards giving up.
Using the wind instead of fighting it. Your old drives aren’t only obstacles. The need to belong can get you studying, if you study with friends. The love of small wins can get you to the gym, if you track your streak. The pull towards status can get you through a hard project, if people are waiting to see it. Trim the sails; don’t fight the weather.
Maybe it isn’t a war
Here’s the part I’d ask you to sit with.
Look at where the far-seeing self is actually steering. Quite often it’s towards the same places the wind was blowing anyway: more money, a bigger title, more respect. It sees further than the cravings do, but it’s often carrying out their orders, just on a longer timeline.
You already know how that tends to go. You get the job, and within months it’s normal and you want the next one. You get the raise, and your spending rises to meet it. Psychologists call this the hedonic treadmill, and I’ve written about it in Why the Age of Abundance Won’t Feel Like One. If you’re reading this on a phone, with a roof over your head, you have more comfort and more choice than almost every human who has ever lived. And still the wanting doesn’t stop. It never does.
I’m not saying your goals are meaningless. Study for the exam, chase the job, go to the gym. Those things matter, and the person who does them usually has a better life than the person who doesn’t. I’m saying something smaller: it isn’t the end of the world if they don’t happen. Hold them a bit more lightly. Be a bit more suspicious of how much they promise. And notice how much you already have, which is what people mean when they talk about gratitude.
So maybe it’s not a war. Maybe it’s a game. In a game you still play hard, you still want to win, and you still get annoyed when you lose. But losing a game isn’t a tragedy, and nobody forgets to enjoy it.
Some of what helps, meditation and patience and using the wind, helps you win. The rest, gratitude and holding goals lightly, helps you see there was less at stake than you thought.
Keep a hand on the tiller. But every now and then, stop fighting the sails, sit back, and look around. You’re on a boat in the middle of the ocean, and the view is incredible.

Mind/What-Is-Ego.title: What Is Ego?
Mind/What-Is-Ego.content:
One word for hurt pride and for what monks try to dissolve, a definition that covers both, and why a weaker ego buys you peace

We use the word ego in two places that seem to have nothing to do with each other.
The first is everyday. “He wasn’t invited to the meeting and his ego took a hit.” “Don’t stroke her ego.” “It’s an ego thing.” Here ego means something close to pride or self-respect: the part of you that wants to be acknowledged, and gets hurt when it isn’t.
The second is spiritual. People talk about ego death, about dissolving the ego, about the ego being what separates you from everything else. When the ego goes, they say, you dissolve into the universe, or into union with nature.
One sounds like office politics and the other like enlightenment. I think they’re the same thing. Pinning it down explains both uses, and explains why so many traditions tell you to make it smaller.
The I-maker
The spiritual meaning is older, so start there. In Indian philosophy the word is ahamkara, which literally means “the I-maker”. It’s the part of the mind that takes this body, and the thoughts and roles that come with it, and says: this is me. Most contemplative traditions have some version of the idea. The details differ, but the core is the same: ego is identifying with one particular person, the one in this body, as me.
On its own that sounds harmless. Of course I’m me. The trouble starts with what comes next.
A bias towards one person
Once you’ve identified with someone, you start favouring them. Here’s my definition:
Ego is a bias that tilts your thinking in favour of the person you identify as. I should be acknowledged. I deserve respect. I’m special. My idea is better. I wasn’t wrong.
Identifying comes first, and favouring follows. Psychologists have names for the favouring: self-serving bias (taking credit for your wins and blaming circumstances for your losses) and egocentric bias (overestimating how much you matter, and how central you are to what’s going on).
That one definition covers both uses of the word. When your ego gets “hurt” or “stroked”, the bias is being threatened or fed. When a monk talks about ego death, it’s the bias switching off: no particular person gets special treatment any more. Same thing, different volume.



EVERYDAY
"my ego was hurt"

SPIRITUAL
"ego death"

fed or threatened
switched off

ONE THING
a bias in favour of "me"


Why call it a bias
A bias is anything that pulls your reasoning away from where the evidence points. Ego does exactly that.
Watch any conversation where egos are involved. It stops being a conversation. People use it to promote themselves, to fish for compliments, to cover up a mistake. Somebody tells a story and somebody else tops it. An argument that should end with “oh, you’re right” goes on for another twenty minutes, because conceding feels like losing. The question itself slips into second place, behind who comes out looking better.
So weakening the ego makes you more rational, almost by definition. Take away the bias and what’s left is the question.
But the traditions make a bigger claim: that a weaker ego makes you more at peace. That one needs an argument.
Why ego costs you peace
First, a concession. Ego does give you highs. When someone with a big ego gets praised, they really do feel great, maybe better in that moment than someone who doesn’t care much. So I won’t argue that a big ego makes you miserable all the time. My claim is narrower: it buys you a few moments, and costs you your baseline. Here’s why.
It’s a zero-sum game. Everybody wants to feel special. But special is relative: you can only be above average if someone else is below it. So it can’t satisfy everyone, and conversations turn into small contests over who’s smarter, more successful, more interesting. Even when you win today, everyone else is still playing.
It’s fragile, and other people feed it. The respect and acknowledgement ego lives on are controlled by somebody else. A word can hurt it. A missing word can hurt it: you weren’t thanked, you weren’t invited, nobody laughed at your joke. Carrying an ego is like walking down a crowded street carrying something made of glass. Every so often it catches the light and it’s lovely. Most of the time you’re just watching for elbows. That constant low hum of vigilance is the opposite of peace. And the bigger the ego, the bigger the glass, and the more people who might bump into it.
The amplifier is lopsided. People feel a loss about twice as strongly as an equal gain; psychologists call this loss aversion. Ego turns up the volume on both. But turning up a scale that’s already tilted makes the tilt bigger. (The tall dashed bar is the other half of the story; more on it below.)







joys the ego
can't reach



+1
−2
+2
−4
small ego
big ego

a win for the ego

an equal loss


The two sides don’t last the same, either. Praise fades within days: you get used to it, and you need more. The threat of being disrespected never fades, because it can come from anyone at any time. Like most of the drives evolution gave us, ego was built to give you a direction, not a destination. It isn’t meant to be filled.
The research points the same way. Psychologists call self-worth that hangs on approval and results contingent self-worth, and people with more of it tend to have more stress and anxiety, and sharper swings up and down.
Isn’t the high worth something?
Say you weaken your ego. You do lose the particular thrill of having it stroked. Does that matter?
Cocaine produces real pleasure too, and nobody thinks you’re missing out by not taking it. It isn’t even a special kind of pleasure. It’s the same feeling, reached by a different route, with a heavy price attached. The ego high is like that. The pleasure at the end is the ordinary kind. You don’t care whether your parcel came by postman or by drone; what matters is that it arrived. If you can get there by a route that doesn’t involve carrying glass through a crowd, you’ve lost nothing.
And the ego’s pleasure has a low ceiling. The best it can offer is feeling a bit more special than the monkey next to you. Now look at what people report from the other end: the moments when the sense of self drops away completely, in deep meditation, in awe, in prayer. They describe them as among the most intense experiences of their lives. Meditators reach for drug words to describe them, and people on psychedelics reach for spiritual words; in clinical studies, the part volunteers most often single out is the dissolving of the self. Whatever you think of those states, the point stands: a smaller ego doesn’t cap your highs. Satisfying your fragile monkey ego is what has the low cap.
And you don’t need a monastery for the everyday version. There’s a lot of pleasure on the other route.
What you get instead
With a weaker ego, the world starts to look like a circus. The petty games we play, the status fights, the outrage of the week, people competing over who’s busiest. It’s very funny, once you’re not anxiously taking part.
Watch a documentary about chimpanzees: the alliances, the displays, the sulking when someone lower down gets the better spot. Then look at an office, a family group chat, a comment section. Then, and this is the important part, look at yourself. When you can see your own version of the chimpanzee display and laugh at it, something lets go. Laughing at yourself is one of the most rewarding things a person can do, and it’s only available when your ego isn’t guarding the door.
There’s also a whole category of suffering that’s hard to even produce without ego. Try being humiliated without a self that matters. Try envy, or wounded pride, or resentment that someone didn’t give you your due. Each of these needs a “me” that’s important. Not all sadness is like this: grieving someone you love isn’t ego. But a lot of the everyday sadness we argue ourselves into runs through “this happened to me, and I deserved better”. Weaken the ego, and those arguments stop being convincing.
Life starts to look less like a test and more like an amusement park.
Weaker, not gone
There’s a reason I defined ego as favouring yourself rather than identifying with yourself.
If ego were the identifying, then getting rid of it would mean no longer knowing which body is yours. Some meditative and spiritual states do go there, and dissolve the sense of self completely. They can be profound, but you can’t run a life from inside one. You need to know whose hands to move and whose rent to pay.
Favouring is different. You can keep “I” as a plain label, a pointer to this particular monkey, and still act, think, plan, want things and work hard. What you drop is the extra weight: the sense that this monkey is special, that everything is a verdict on it, that the stakes are always enormous. You keep the ability to act. You lose the ability to make everything feel serious and daunting.
It isn’t all or nothing, either. You aren’t one fixed self, the same in every moment. There’s the version of you that’s competing in a meeting, the one that’s relaxed with old friends, the one sitting quietly in the morning. Some carry more ego than others. The aim isn’t to make every one of them egoless. It’s to turn the volume down on average, so the version that shows up most often is carrying less glass. Think of an orchestra rather than a soloist: lots of players, some louder than others, and the job is to make the music good, not to silence everyone. (I’ve written about this way of seeing the self in Microframeworks, but you don’t need it here.)
Where this lands
Ego is the I-maker plus a bias: first you take this person to be you, then your thinking tilts in their favour. That tilt is what gets “hurt” in the office and what “dies” in the monastery.
Its highs are real. But it’s a zero-sum game, played with something fragile, fed by other people, and tuned to feel losses more than gains. Turning it down costs you a few small peaks, gives you back your baseline, and opens up highs the ego can’t reach. It also gets you the best seat in the circus, including for the act where you’re the clown.

Philosophy/Logic-Isn't-About-Truth.title: Logic Isn't About Truth
Philosophy/Logic-Isn't-About-Truth.content:
What it costs to mistake logic for a truth machine

Most people treat logic as a machine for finding the truth: feed in facts, turn the handle, and truth comes out the other end. I think that’s wrong, and the mistake is expensive. It’s behind cults, behind smug atheism, behind half the pointless arguments on the internet, and behind a lot of quiet guilt people carry about being “inconsistent”.
I’ve written about what logic is in What Is Logic. The short version: you start from axioms, extend them in language into a framework, and keep the framework coherent so it keeps predicting. This piece is about what logic isn’t, and what it costs to get that wrong.
Maths: the model that outgrows its source
Mathematics shows what a framework can do better than anything else. Counting starts as a mirror: three sheep, three pebbles. Numbers are abstract, but they’re mapped to something real. Algebra, calculus and differential equations are built further along the same road, from observations of quantity, change and motion.
Then maths does something stranger. Once you have a model, you can extend it past anything that exists. No number multiplied by itself gives −1. Mathematicians in the 1500s assumed one anyway, later called it i, and kept every other rule the same. They did it to solve equations, not to describe shapes.
And the made-up thing mapped back onto reality, somewhere nobody expected. Multiplying by i turns out to be a quarter turn, so complex numbers became a language for rotation and geometry, then for alternating current, and eventually for quantum mechanics. The foundations weren’t taken from geometry at all, and yet the result describes geometry. The physicist Eugene Wigner called this “the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics”. To me it’s the most beautiful thing about the subject: build an honest model, follow its rules past the edge of what you’ve seen, and it sometimes finds things before you do.
Why you never reach absolute truth
Every model starts from observation, and observation is limited. The limit that matters most is time.
To know something is absolutely true, you’d have to watch it hold across all of time. You can’t; you only ever see a stretch of it. Bertrand Russell’s chicken is the classic picture. The farmer feeds it every morning, and every morning the chicken’s model of the world is confirmed again, right up to the morning he wrings its neck.
So every claim about the world, however well tested, is a hypothesis. David Hume saw this in the 1700s. Karl Popper later built a philosophy of science on it: one clear failure can disprove a theory, but no number of successes can finally prove it.
Logic is a motion, not a position
If logic can’t hand you absolute truth, what is it? I think of it as a motion rather than a position. Logic isn’t a piece of information. It’s how you move through information: how you extend it, and how you get new information out of what you already have.
You start with axioms, apply rules of inference (if A implies B, and B implies C, then A implies C), and what grows out of that is a framework.
The axioms have only a couple of requirements. They shouldn’t contradict each other, and ideally none of them should follow from the others. Nothing requires them to come from reality. We’ve already seen that: √−1 is nonsense as a fact about the world, and the framework built on it is one of the most useful things humans own.
Look across the sciences and it’s the same shape every time:

Physics: make observations, build a framework from them, use it to predict.
Mathematics: choose axioms (often observations in disguise), build a framework, and it predicts, sometimes in fields it was never meant for.
Biology, and the rest of science: observe, model, predict, revise.

Logicians have a precise way to say this. An argument is valid if the conclusion follows from the premises. It’s sound if it’s valid and the premises are true. “All cats can fly; Tom is a cat; so Tom can fly” is perfectly valid and completely unsound. Logic only guarantees validity. Truth has to come in from outside, through the premises, and logic can’t check them for you.
That leads somewhere surprising: it’s very hard to be illogical. However much nonsense someone talks, they’re still chaining one thing to another, A to B to C. Even a bare claim with nothing derived from it is a framework, just one with a single node. When we call someone illogical, we usually mean one of two things: they’re reasoning from axioms we don’t share, or one of their steps doesn’t follow.
The cost of not knowing
Truth stops being the point
Physics isn’t supposed to be true. It’s supposed to predict. Newton’s laws are, strictly speaking, wrong; Einstein replaced them. Engineers still use them every day, because within their range they predict superbly. The statistician George Box put it best: “All models are wrong, but some are useful.”
Being closer to the truth usually helps a framework do its job, and that’s exactly why people confuse the two. Truth correlates with good logic, but it isn’t what makes reasoning logical. And sometimes the two come far apart, especially in philosophy and in relationships, where the most accurate thing isn’t always the best thing. Telling someone their cooking is mediocre on the night they cook for you may be true. It’s not what the evening is for.
This was the first big unlock for me. Once philosophy didn’t have to be true, I could point it at what I actually want from it, which is peace, and optimise for that directly. It’s working out really well. It lets me hold beliefs like nothing is all that serious, which has a nihilistic edge, without defending them as facts about the universe. They only have to do their job. (You can make truth the goal of a philosophy. You just have to choose it explicitly.) I’ve worked this out at length in Microframeworks.
Cults and the clever atheist make the same mistake
People get pulled into cults by someone claiming to know the absolute truth. Sometimes that person is a liar, and sometimes they’re sincerely fooled by their own brain. Either way, they’re using a relative instrument to sell an absolute. If you understand what logic is, you’ll never try to prove God with it, in the sense of establishing a final fact.
The other side makes the same mistake in reverse, using science to “prove” that religion is nonsense. I was one of them as a teenager: I’m so scientific, so logical, and all this religion and spirituality is unscientific bullshit. I was the clown there. I’d taken logic for a truth machine and was waving it at people.
Judged by usefulness, by what it predicts or how much peace it brings, God can be perfectly logical. Belief may have brought order to societies when it arose. Human brains relate to idols, and idolising motivates. Some feelings may only be available to people who believe. Decode the psychology and you could probably justify much of the value belief brings. The cultist and the clever atheist end up where they are for the same reason: they think logic is about truth.
One case against a general claim
This one is so common it drives me up the wall, and it runs both ways.
A counterexample against a tendency. You say “smoking generally shortens your life”, and someone replies “my grandfather smoked forty a day and lived to ninety-five”. When did I say always? A counterexample destroys a universal claim: one black swan and nobody can say “all swans are white” again. It barely dents a statistical one. One grandfather doesn’t move the curve.
A single case turned into a rule. The reverse is just as common. One bad meal and the restaurant is terrible. One friend’s startup fails and startups are a scam. One instance shows that something can happen. It says almost nothing about how often.
Both mistakes come from the same gap: not seeing that “always”, “usually” and “once” are different kinds of claim, which need different kinds of evidence.
You’re allowed to be more than one framework
This last one looks like a different topic, but it grows from the same root, and it’s the reason I can enjoy dark humour.
People feel a strong pull to fit their whole life into one consistent framework, because hypocrisy feels repulsive. So they enforce it on others: you laughed at a joke about someone in hospital, so you’re insensitive. That only works if a person is one belief system, one constitution, one truth.
A person isn’t. A person is a mix of many frameworks, and our wiring couldn’t hold to just one even if we tried. You can laugh at dark humour and still be kind, just as someone who eats meat can still have deep empathy. You don’t owe anyone a reconciliation. Walt Whitman got there first: “Do I contradict myself? Very well then I contradict myself, (I am large, I contain multitudes.)”
A lot of cognitive dissonance, the discomfort of holding beliefs that seem to clash, comes from thinking that being logical means having one framework. It doesn’t. Your beliefs can depend on context. What makes them look contradictory is that the context has been stripped out. Put it back, and they often fit inside one larger framework that is perfectly consistent.

Logic is a way of moving, not a place to arrive. Once you know that, you stop asking it for what it can’t give you, which is certainty, and use it for what it’s good at: getting you, one step at a time, wherever you’ve decided to go.
