Philosophy/Microframeworks.content:
There’s no single “you” in charge, and peace doesn’t have to wait


                  
                  Background 
                  
                

Some of the groundwork is in separate pieces, linked along the way. You don’t need to read them first.



Think about the thing you’re working towards right now: a job, an exam, a house, a person. There’s probably a sentence that comes with it. Once this is done, I can relax.
This whole philosophy comes from taking one question about that sentence seriously:

If you’ll be at peace once you’ve done this thing, why can’t you be at peace first, and then do it?

It sounds like a trick question. I don’t think it is. To answer it, I had to work out what we’re actually chasing, and then take apart the idea that there’s a single “you” doing the chasing.
What we’re chasing: peace, not happiness
The obvious answer is happiness. I think that answer is a correlation mistaken for a cause.
Most of the time, happiness and peace arrive together. You get the job, you feel happy, and for a while you stop wanting anything to change. Pain usually arrives with struggle: you want it gone. Because the pairs show up together so reliably, we assume happiness is what produces peace. Get happy, and peace will follow. So we chase happiness.
But look at the moments where the two come apart. We watch sad films. We eat food so spicy it hurts, ride roller coasters, and stand in a stadium screaming, heart pounding, in something close to rage. All of these feel bad by any emotional measure. And yet, in the middle of them, we don’t want them to stop.
That last part is the test. It isn’t pain now for a reward later, like an ice bath you endure for the glow afterwards. It’s discomfort while not wanting things to be any different. That is what I mean by peace: not struggling against whatever you’re experiencing.






unpleasant
pleasant
struggling → at peace


getting what you want

pain you want gone

a spicy meala sad filma roller coaster
they usually move together, but not always


If peace can show up alongside discomfort, then happiness isn’t what produces it. The two usually travel together, and that’s all. Peace isn’t a particular feeling; it’s a relationship to whatever you’re feeling, and sadness can have it as easily as joy. So if what we’re really after is the peace, then chasing happiness means chasing the thing that usually comes along with it, and hoping.
I don’t need to claim that everyone secretly wants peace. A weaker claim is enough. Plenty of people look honestly at their lives and notice the loop: want something, get it, settle for a while, want the next thing. (I’ve written about that loop, the hedonic treadmill, in Why the Age of Abundance Won’t Feel Like One.) If that loop doesn’t satisfy you, peace is something you can aim at directly, instead of hoping it arrives at the end of a list.
The usual picture: you versus your mind
Ask how people try to get there and you’ll usually hear some version of one picture. There’s you, the part that plans and sees far, and there’s your mind, the cravings and moods that keep dragging you off course. Discipline is you winning; failure is your mind winning. I wrote about that picture in The War Between You and Your Mind, and for everyday purposes I think it’s a good one.
For a long time, it was my whole philosophy. Then, taken all the way, it started producing two problems.
The first was frustration that never ends. Why can’t I just take control? Why do I need tricks? Worse, it poisoned good experiences after the fact. I’d work passionately for hours, and afterwards a voice would say: that wasn’t really you, that was ambition. Every experience became an interrogation of motives.
The second was paralysis. Once I decided most worldly goals were driven by “the mind”, my motivation for ordinary goals drained away. But the cravings I’d written off didn’t stop. They kept running my days, just without my approval.
A philosophy meant to bring peace had become a reliable source of guilt. So I went back and looked more carefully at the “I” at the centre of it.
There’s no single you
Take a sentence like “I didn’t want to do it, but my mind made me.” Afterwards we say “that wasn’t me.” Who is the “I” in each half of that sentence?
Physically, there’s no separate self and no separate mind. There’s one system, a brain and body reacting to the world. “Self” and “mind” are labels we draw over its behaviour, and the line between them moves. Whatever we disapprove of afterwards gets moved to the other side.
There’s a striking piece of evidence for how loosely the “I” sits on top. In some patients whose brain halves have been surgically separated, you can show an instruction to only the half that can’t speak, and the patient carries it out. Ask the speaking half why they did it, and it doesn’t say “I don’t know.” It invents a confident, reasonable-sounding explanation on the spot. The part that narrates isn’t the part that decides; it’s the part that explains.
Microframeworks
So if there’s no single self, what is the “I” that wants things?
Watch it across one day. In the morning, I want to work hard. By afternoon I want a break. In the evening I want company, and at midnight I want one more video. Each of these comes with its own priorities, its own sense of what matters, and its own idea of who “I” am. They don’t feel like moods of one fixed person. They feel like different people taking turns to say “I”.




the spotlight moves on its own




I want towork hardI needa breakI wantcompanyone morevideo


morningafternooneveningmidnight
each one says "I"


I call each of these a microframework: a small, temporary set of assumptions, plus whatever information happens to be in view, plus its own meaning for the word “I”. “Framework” is meant in the logician’s sense, as a set of starting assumptions and everything that follows from them (see What Is Logic). The “micro” is because they’re small and short-lived. What really separates one from another is what it takes for granted. “I need a break” and “I want to work hard” aren’t arguing from the same starting point, which is why they never convince each other.
That also settles what counts as one framework: a framework is defined by its axioms, its starting assumptions. You rarely think about them while you’re inside it, but every bit of reasoning you do starts from some, so it always belongs to some framework. In the moment, you can’t see the edges. Looking back, you always can. The moment “I need a break” took over from “I want to work hard” is the moment the starting assumptions changed. And they’re micro because they don’t last: a few minutes, an hour, an evening.
Two images help me hold this.
A spotlight. Picture all the ways you could think about your life as a huge dark stage, and a spotlight that lights up one small part at a time. You don’t choose where it goes. Your surroundings, your memories, how much you slept, and what you scrolled past all move it. Even “choosing” happens inside whichever part is lit at the time.
Peripheral vision. Your eyes only see sharply in a small area; the rest is blur. Inside a framework it’s the same. You reason sharply about a few things, while most of your assumptions sit blurry at the edges, never examined.
What changes when you see it this way
You plan for your future changes of mind. If the “I” making a plan isn’t a permanent manager, plan for the one who’ll be in charge later. Deleting Instagram from your phone isn’t an admission of weakness. It’s sensible preparation by a framework that knows a different one will be running at eleven tonight.
Regret loses its sting. The “I” judging yesterday’s mistake has different priorities from the “I” that made it. “I had no self-control” is one framework’s opinion of another, with no special authority. You didn’t fail at being yourself. You were a different you.
But it isn’t a free pass. All these frameworks share one body, and what one does shapes the next. One framework finds peace in a whole pizza at midnight, and the morning framework wakes up sluggish and anxious. That’s what I mean by karma: not cosmic bookkeeping, just consequences passed from one framework to the next through the body they share. Discipline still matters. It just works by shaping conditions, not by an inner commander winning a fight.
Things matter, locally
Where do our purposes come from? Upbringing, culture, personal history, and the survival instincts evolution put in us. Seeing that doesn’t make a purpose false. You can know exactly why you love your family and love them just as much.
But it does change how much authority a purpose gets. Here’s my position, as precisely as I can put it: everything that matters, matters inside some framework. Brushing your teeth matters a lot to the framework doing it, and very little to the one planning your year. Your country matters intensely to the patriotic one. None of that is fake. What I deny is that any purpose matters outside every framework, written into the universe and binding on everyone. Things matter locally. Nothing is commanded absolutely. (Why I’m comfortable judging beliefs by usefulness instead of final truth is in Logic Isn’t About Truth.)
This is what I mean by creating distance from a purpose. You don’t stop caring. You see the scope of the care: where it came from, which frameworks it lives in, and the fact that your peace doesn’t have to wait for it.
You can take that distance at different depths:

Keep the purpose fully, and see whether caring a little less about the outcome makes you steadier, and better at it.
Look at where it came from, and loosen how much of your identity rests on it.
Make peace itself your main aim, and keep the other purposes as commitments you choose.

Picture a soldier who keeps serving their country while knowing their patriotism was taught, not discovered. They still serve. They’re just not at war with every setback.
The orchestrator
Something in you is reading this and thinking about how to live better. I call it the orchestrator: the frameworks that understand all of this and try to coordinate the rest.
It isn’t a manager outside the system; that would just bring back the single self. It runs on the same brain as everything else, and it comes and goes like any other framework. Tonight the spotlight will move and the orchestrator will go dark. That’s expected.
The difference from the old picture is one sentence: the old self believed its “I”. The orchestrator uses its “I”. The war model took “me” as a fact. There really was a war, and a self who ought to win, so every loss was a real failure and guilt was built in. The orchestrator treats “I” as a working assumption, the way a mathematician treats the square root of minus one: it doesn’t exist as an ordinary number, and it’s enormously useful anyway. When another framework takes over, “that was a different I” is already part of the plan. There’s nothing to feel guilty about.
Its job is coordination, not control. Think of the frameworks as employees: the ambitious one, the caring one, the curious one, the one who wants a nap. A good company doesn’t need them all to share one personality. It needs them pulling in roughly the same direction instead of sabotaging each other. The orchestrator is the manager, and it works mostly through conditions: what you learn, what you surround yourself with, which triggers you remove, and which good habits you make easy.
And its wanting is different. The orchestrator wants the rest of the system to be at peace, and wanting is still wanting. But it’s wanting the way you want to win a game you’re enjoying: full engagement, nothing missing. Not wanting from lack, but wanting as play.
Living it: distance without losing the drive
There’s an obvious cost here, and I won’t pretend otherwise. Distance works against motivation. If you decide nothing matters absolutely and then try to act, you won’t act with the hunger of someone who’s certain the next promotion is everything. A greedy person with no doubts will outwork a detached one.
The way out isn’t to pick one framework and force the rest to agree with it. That’s the cognitive dissonance that made the war model so exhausting. The way out is to let all of them in. Hindu thought has a word for this: lila, play. Krishna knows the whole cosmic drama is a drama, and plays every role in it with complete passion anyway.
That’s how the orchestrator relates to the frameworks. Each employee takes its own goal completely seriously, and it should, because that’s where the drive comes from. The ambitious one really wants the promotion. The caring one really wants the family to be all right. The orchestrator doesn’t need to share their seriousness. It decides who’s on shift today, and keeps their goals lined up with the company’s. The detachment sits with the manager; the drive stays with the employees. That’s how you get distance and motivation together.
In practice, this is the old Indian idea of karma yoga: work fully towards your goals, and hold the outcomes lightly.
Some practical consequences:

Let every motive help. Ambition, curiosity, affection and enjoyment are all fuel. The goal isn’t to suppress them; it’s to point them in compatible directions.
Prepare for the spotlight to move. Change your surroundings, remove predictable triggers, make good responses easy. That’s engineering, not weakness.
Treat frustration as a signal. When you catch yourself condemning a past action, look at the conditions that produced it, and change those.
Expect to forget all this. You’ll get absorbed, lose the outlook, and get lost in the chase again. That doesn’t disprove it. The outlook spreads slowly across many frameworks, never all at once.

This also explains why nobody gets perfectly disciplined, however much they practise. Practice changes where the spotlight tends to land. It never pins it in place, because nobody is holding it. Push hard enough (real pain, real fear) and it gets dragged regardless. You can shift the odds; you can’t freeze them.
It even explains what reading something like this does. It isn’t instructions to some boss standing outside the system, because there’s no such boss. It’s conditioning. It makes frameworks like the orchestrator light up a little more often.
My choice: optimistic nihilism
So where does this leave purpose? Plainly: I’m an optimistic nihilist. There’s no inherent purpose, nothing that has to be done. Whatever goal I hold is a choice, and an arbitrary one.
That includes the bigger ideas. A universal self, or a soul everyone shares, is a useful concept that frameworks inside this body came up with, not a fact I discovered. I’ll write about that separately.
Since the choice is arbitrary anyway, I made one: not to be steered by ego, the bias that puts this one body at the centre of everything. So I define my goal, loosely, as the well-being of people in general. And I’m not very serious about it. The roles I play might be: the engineer about the product, the friend about their friends, the citizen about the country. Each of them pursues its own goal, sometimes fiercely. The orchestrator only does the manager’s job, keeping the employees’ goals pointed roughly where the company is going.
That’s not a doctrine to defend. It’s a choice I made, and you’re free to make a different one.
So, back to the question: if you’ll be at peace once you’ve done this thing, why can’t you be at peace first, and then do it?
My answer is that you can. Not by winning the war with your mind, but by noticing that the one who’d win it was never a single person. Do the thing, fully. Just don’t make your peace wait for it.

Philosophy/The-Soul-Is-a-Product-of-Ego.title: The Soul Is a Product of Ego
Philosophy/The-Soul-Is-a-Product-of-Ego.content:
Why the usual picture of the soul looks like the ego’s handiwork, and why I still believe in a soul anyway

Ask most people what a soul is and you get roughly the same picture. There’s a light inside the body. It’s what makes the body alive, and when it leaves, the body is just a body. Each of us has one. It carries who we are, and in many traditions it goes on after we die.
I’m going to argue that this picture was made by the ego. Then, at the end, I’ll tell you why I still believe in a soul. Just not that one.
A name in the sand
I can’t prove this, so let me be clear about what kind of claim it is.
Say you’re walking on a beach and you find a name written in the sand. It’s possible that wind and waves happened to leave that exact pattern. You can’t strictly rule it out. But nobody believes it. The far likelier story is that someone was here with a stick. You don’t need to have seen them. The pattern gives them away, because it looks like the kind of thing people make.


                  
                  A fairer version 
                  
                

A name is almost impossible to get by accident, so it makes my case sound stronger than it is. A fairer example is a face. Nature does make faces sometimes: the famous “face on Mars” turned out to be a hill and some shadows, and people see faces in clouds and on the Moon all the time (psychologists call this pareidolia). So a face in the sand isn’t proof. But if you found one on a beach, you’d still bet on a person. That’s the strength of my claim: not proof, a strong lean.


The usual soul has a pattern like that. In What Is Ego? I described ego as the I-maker: the part of the mind that takes this body to be me, and then tilts everything in its favour. Now look at the soul. There’s exactly one per body. It’s mine. It carries my memories and my personality. It’s what makes me special among animals. And in many versions it survives my death, which is the one thing the body can’t do.
That’s the shape the ego would draw if it were drawing a soul.
I can’t make a logical case against something that, by definition, isn’t made of anything we can measure. What I can do is show why the odds lean one way. The rest of this piece is that.
A default, not a conclusion
First, notice that almost nobody reasons their way to a soul. It’s there before any reasoning starts.
Young children, in every culture psychologists have studied, assume that a person has a mind or spirit that’s separate from the body, without anyone teaching them. Psychologists call this intuitive dualism. It’s one of the defaults we’re born with, like the way people all over the world smile the same way when they’re happy.
Defaults like this have explanations. For a social animal, it pays to treat yourself and others as someone inside, with plans and feelings, because that’s how you predict what they’ll do next. So the feeling that there’s a light inside is exactly what a brain built by evolution would produce, whether or not the light is really there. That doesn’t make the feeling wrong. It does mean the feeling isn’t evidence.
So let’s look at the picture itself.
Blurring the boundary of the body
What does it even mean for the soul to be in the body? Two things seem to define “inside”: what I can control, and what I can feel.
Control is the easy one. I can move my hand. I can also move the cup on that table; it just takes a few more steps. The difference is distance, and distance is only one of the limits matter puts on me. I can’t move a cup in the United States from here. But I also can’t bend my hand backwards, and that hand is supposedly full of soul. Matter has its limits inside the skin and outside it. Control doesn’t stop at the skin in any special way.
Feeling is the stronger case. Pinch the cup and I feel nothing. Pinch my hand and I do. Surely that’s where I end?
Go one level down and look at what feeling is. Every experience is a chain of changes passing through matter. Light leaves the sun, bounces off the cup, enters the eye, becomes a signal in a nerve and reaches the brain. A pin presses the skin, a signal travels up a nerve and through the spinal cord, and reaches the brain. The hand is one link in a chain, just like the cup. Nothing special happens at the skin. The chain just passes through it.
Where you feel something is a separate question, and the brain decides it. It places every sense somewhere. Sound seems to be out there, where it came from. Sight comes with depth, laid out across the room. Touch and pain get placed on a map the brain keeps of the body. So touch isn’t the soul filling the body. It’s one sense among several, and its map happens to be shaped like the body. The others use a map of your surroundings.



MAP OF THE SURROUNDINGS
sound

sight
with depth

BODY MAP

brain
touch, pain

rubber hand


That map lines up with the body, for obvious practical reasons. But it isn’t tied to the flesh, and you can show it.

The rubber hand illusion. Hide someone’s real hand behind a screen and put a rubber hand in front of them. Stroke both with a brush at the same moment. After a minute or two, many people start to feel the brush on the rubber hand. Then bring a hammer down on the rubber hand. People flinch, and their stress response jumps, as if it were their own.
Phantom limbs. Many people who’ve lost an arm or a leg still feel it, and some feel pain in it for years. The map kept a hand the body no longer has.
A numbed hand. After a nerve block, or a spinal injury, a hand can be completely alive: fed by blood, warm, able to heal. And it drops out of experience entirely.

That last one goes straight at the picture we started with. “Alive” and “felt” come apart. The light that supposedly makes the body alive and the light of experience aren’t the same thing, and neither fills the body edge to edge.
So whatever experiences, it isn’t spread through the body like light through a lamp. It’s concentrated wherever the maps are kept, and the edge of the body is one of the things it projects. The skin isn’t the soul’s border. It’s the ego’s.
A single point?
The obvious retreat is: fine, the soul isn’t body-shaped. It’s a point. The one place where everything comes together, where I see and I decide. Philosophers have tried exactly this; one famous attempt put the soul in a single small gland in the middle of the brain.
So let’s test the point.
Where does the line fall?
Start with animals, because this one you already feel.
You’ve looked a dog in the eye and known someone was home. You’ve watched a cat startle, a crow solve a puzzle, an elephant stand over a dead companion. At some point most of us have felt it: they’re alive the way we’re alive. That’s why cruelty to them makes us flinch.
And yet many traditions draw a hard line. Humans have souls; animals don’t, or have lesser ones. For centuries, serious thinkers argued that animals were machines that only looked as though they felt pain. People still argue about whether fish feel anything.
Look at where that line falls. Biologically, we’re astonishingly close to the animals around us. A chimpanzee shares almost all of our DNA. A dog’s brain has the same basic parts as ours, running on the same chemistry. Nervous systems shade into each other smoothly, from worms to fish to mice to dogs to apes to us, and there’s no step anywhere on that slope where something new switches on. In 2012, a group of prominent neuroscientists signed a public declaration that many animals, including all mammals and birds, have what it takes for conscious experience.
And the soul was never supposed to be about intelligence in the first place. It’s the light that makes something alive and feeling. On that, the dog and you are on the same footing.


a smooth slope,
no step anywhere


wormfishmousedogchimphuman

we drew the soul line here


So where do you draw the line? You don’t, because there isn’t one. The only place it has ever been drawn is right around us, and we’re the ones who drew it. A line that falls exactly where it flatters the one drawing it is the name in the sand again.
Seeing without knowing
Now go inside a single human head.
Some people with damage to the visual part of the brain go blind in part of their field of view. Ask them and they’ll tell you, honestly, that they see nothing there. But put an object in that blind area and ask them to guess where it is, and they point to it far more often than chance would allow. One such patient, blind by his own account, walked down a corridor cluttered with obstacles and stepped around every one of them. This is called blindsight.
Something in that person saw, and it guided their body. The “I” who talks had no idea. If the soul is the single point where seeing happens, which one is it: the part that saw, or the part that says it didn’t?
Two halves, one story
The clearest case comes from surgery.
For some people with severe epilepsy, surgeons used to cut the thick bundle of fibres that connects the two halves of the brain. The patients recovered well and seemed completely normal. But careful experiments showed that the two halves could no longer share what they knew.
Two facts make the experiment work. Each half of the brain sees one side of what you’re looking at and controls the opposite hand. And in most people, only the left half can talk.
In one famous test, a patient was shown two pictures at once, one to each half. The left half saw a chicken’s foot. The right half saw a snowy scene. Then he was asked to pick, from a row of cards, the ones that went with what he’d seen. His right hand, run by the left half, picked a chicken. His left hand, run by the right half, picked a shovel, for the snow.
Then he was asked why he’d picked the shovel.
The talking half had never seen the snow. It had no idea why the left hand did what it did. And without a moment’s hesitation he said: “Oh, that’s simple. The chicken claw goes with the chicken, and you need a shovel to clean out the chicken shed.”

He wasn’t lying, and he wasn’t confused. The talking half had a gap, filled it instantly with a reasonable story, and believed the story. In another version, the silent half was shown the word “walk”, and the patient got up and started walking. Asked where he was going, he said he wanted to get a drink. The scientists who ran these studies gave the storyteller in the left half a name: the interpreter.
It isn’t only split brains
You could say these are damaged brains. But healthy brains do the same thing all the time.
In table tennis, the ball comes at you faster than your eyes can guide a return. Your brain predicts where the ball will be and starts the swing before you’ve consciously seen it arrive. Afterwards, it feels as though you saw the ball and decided to hit it. Kurzgesagt has a good video on this, Why Your Brain Blinds You For 2 Hours Every Day: your body handles a lot of decisions on its own, and you get told about them a little late.
Or take an experiment on what psychologists call choice blindness. People were shown two photos of faces and asked which one they found more attractive. Then the experimenter handed them their chosen photo and asked why they’d picked it. Except sometimes, with a sleight of hand, it was the other photo. Most people didn’t notice. They explained why they’d chosen it, sometimes pointing to features, like earrings, that only the photo they’d rejected had.
Put it together. The “I” that seems to see everything and decide everything is, much of the time, a narrator that arrives after the fact. It explains decisions made elsewhere, using information it doesn’t have, and it believes its own explanations. Psychologists call this post hoc rationalisation, or in its more extreme forms, confabulation. The single point where everything comes together turns out to be a story the brain tells afterwards.
And the hero of that story is always “me”. That’s the ego’s favourite story.
When the soul goes supernatural
In What Is Ego? I covered what ego costs us day to day: fragile pride, conversations turned into contests. When the ego-shaped soul gets taken for something supernatural, the costs get stranger.
Take astrology. Stars many light years away, burning for billions of years, are supposedly arranged to tell one particular monkey whether Tuesday is a good day for a job interview. Numerology says the same about the digits in your birth date. It’s hard to imagine a belief more flattering to the self: the universe is about me.
And it traps spiritual people too, sometimes more than anyone. Someone does the hard work. They meditate for years, step back from money and status, and get free of a big part of the ego. Then they start claiming they can levitate, or read minds, or perform miracles. The ego didn’t go anywhere. It moved, from the body to the soul. “I’m not this body, I’m a soul, and my soul is special.” There’s even a name for this: spiritual materialism, the ego using spiritual practice to build itself back up.
Or look at the usual picture of enlightenment: someone weeping with bliss, lost in ecstasy. There’s nothing wrong with those experiences. I argued in What Is Ego? that some of the most intense highs a person can have come when the sense of self drops away. The trap is chasing them, and treating them as proof you’ve arrived. That’s the same chase you set out to escape, in robes this time.
The flip side is just as common. Some people decide pleasure is dangerous and action binds you, so they back away from both, afraid that enjoying anything will create attachment and attachment will create suffering. Chasing bliss and fearing pleasure look like opposites, but they share a root. Both are completely absorbed in the fate of one particular soul. A lot of the people who’ve worked hardest to escape the ego end up more preoccupied with themselves than anyone. (Fear of attachment deserves its own piece, and I’ll come back to it.)
Why I still believe in a soul
So do I think there’s no soul? No. I don’t believe there’s an object called a soul sitting inside the body, or waiting in some other dimension. But I do believe in a soul, and here’s why.
Reasoning is a tool, and tools serve purposes. In physics and maths, the purpose is matching reality, and those fields are so successful that we’ve come to think matching reality is what reasoning is for. It isn’t always. A lot of good reasoning aims at something else. You don’t tell a grieving friend every true thing you know. A good therapist nudges people with stories before they’re ready for facts. Parents tell children things that aren’t literally true to help them grow. “Reasoning usually aims at truth” became “reasoning is about truth”: a correlation mistaken for a cause. (More on this in Logic Isn’t About Truth.)
The idea of a soul was made by the mind, which was made by evolution. That doesn’t mean we have to fight it, or tear it down and go hard materialist. In The War Between You and Your Mind I described being born on a sailboat: you can’t stop the wind, but you can use it. Evolution pointed our instruments at survival. We can point the same instruments at whatever we’re actually after. For me, that’s peace.
The mind also has a soft spot I find useful. It responds far better to a person than to a principle. Psychologists call the habit of giving human form to things anthropomorphism. Most of us learn our morals from stories, not lists. You can memorise a list of virtues, or you can read the stories of Krishna, get attached to him, feel something, and find the lessons much easier to live by. (I think God is useful in the same way, and I don’t believe in God as the literal creator of the world either. That’s another piece.)
So I don’t throw the soul away. I split it in two:

The vitality: the sense that experience is alive, that it matters, that there’s something it’s like to be here. That part is good.
The localisation: the soul in this body, mine, one per person. That’s the part the ego feeds on.

I keep the first and drop the second. We’ve already seen that nothing pins experience to the edges of the body. And if the soul isn’t pinned to one body, there’s no reason to think there’s one per body. So I spread it over everything. One soul, not many. This is the old idea of non-duality. Its best-known version, Advaita Vedanta, says the self in you and the reality underneath everything are one and the same, and that the feeling of being a separate soul is exactly the ego’s confusion.
Then why do I only feel this body?
The obvious objection: if my soul is spread across the universe, why do I only experience what happens to this body?
My answer is that the soul, in this sense, doesn’t act, and it doesn’t speak. Everything that reports, everything that says “I see red” or “my hand hurts”, is the body: matter taking in information and putting it back out. And the body can only report on what passed through it.
Think about looking at something red. One part of the story is the body’s: light hits the eye, the brain sorts it, and you can say “red” and tell it apart from green. A machine could do that much. The other part is what the red is like, the redness itself. Philosophers call that quality qualia, and nobody knows how matter produces it. That quality, the living part of experience, is what I call soul. And nothing ties it to this one body. The body just can’t talk about anything else, because the soul never talks at all.
So the body isn’t the living thing with a light inside. It’s an instrument, moving through a world that’s alive everywhere. That’s what ego death feels like from the inside: not losing yourself, but noticing that “yourself” was drawn far too small.
Where this lands
The usual soul, a light inside the body, one per person, mine, special, surviving me, has the ego’s fingerprints all over it. It’s a default we’re born with rather than a conclusion we reached. Its border is the brain’s body map, which a rubber hand can fool. The single point where it supposedly sees and decides keeps turning out to be a narrator telling a story afterwards. And the line it draws between us and the animals falls exactly where it flatters us.
None of that proves there’s no soul. It shows where the odds lean, the same way a name in the sand does.
What I keep is the part worth keeping: the sense that experience is alive and matters, without the fence around one body. I don’t hold that as a fact about the universe. I hold it because it’s useful: it lets me keep the wonder and drop the self-importance.

Philosophy/What-Is-Information.title: What Is Information?
Philosophy/What-Is-Information.content:
Start with the obvious answer, find what’s wrong with it, and keep going

Here’s a question that sounds easy: what is information?
We use the word all the time. We look information up, we worry about having too much of it, we say we live in the information age. But try to say what it actually is and it slips away. For some reason this topic is very hard for the brain to hold on to. Every time I think I’ve got a definition, something about it feels off.
In Logic Isn’t About Truth I described logic as a way of moving through information. This piece is about the thing underneath: the information itself. I’ll start with the obvious answer, find what’s wrong with it, fix it, and repeat. Where I end up is stranger than where I started, but I think it’s closer to the truth, and the way there is the interesting part.
First try: a picture in your head
Start with where the idea of information lives: in my head. And when I look at what else is in my head, I find a rough copy of the world.
Get up at night and walk to the kitchen without turning on the light. You don’t walk into the door frame, because you aren’t relying on your eyes. You’re walking through a copy of your house that you carry around. You know where the counter starts and where the step is, and the copy is good enough that your body trusts it.
That’s what makes the copy useful. I can move things around inside it and find out what would happen outside, without trying it for real. So here’s the face-value answer: information is a picture in a mind that lets it predict the world.
It fits most of what we call information. What you know about your friends, your city, your job: all of it is a copy you check before you act.
Second try: it doesn’t need a mind
Here’s the problem. By that definition, information can’t exist unless a mind is holding it.
Picture a notebook written by someone who died a hundred years ago. Nobody alive has what’s in it in their head. Is it information? Obviously. Open it and it tells you about the world. A map is the same: it still shows where the road bends, long after the person who drew it is gone.
So the mind isn’t the important part. What matters is that the map has something in common with the land. The map is a small pattern, ink on paper, with the same layout as a big pattern, roads on the ground. Because their shapes match, reading one tells you about the other.
Second try, then: information is a pattern, anywhere, whose shape matches another pattern well enough that you can learn about one from the other.
Notice what happened to the line the first try drew between the mind and the world. It’s gone. The notebook isn’t outside reality looking in. It’s a stack of paper in a drawer, part of the world like everything else. So is your brain. Information isn’t something that stands apart from reality and describes it. It’s one part of reality that resembles another part.
Third try: it doesn’t need a reader
There’s still someone hiding in that definition: me. “You can learn about one from the other.” Who’s doing the learning? If nobody ever opens the notebook, does it stop being information?
Think about a tree. Every year it adds a ring, wide in good years and narrow in dry ones. For three hundred years nobody looks. Then the tree comes down, someone counts the rings, and reads off three centuries of rainfall.
Did counting the rings put the information there? No. The rings matched the weather the whole time. The person who counted them only noticed something that was already true.
That’s how you take yourself out of the definition. Calling something information doesn’t change it. It only says how I’m using it, the way a stone becomes a “paperweight” when I put it on my papers. Take me away, and the pattern is still there, still matching whatever made it. If my label is what makes it information, it was information before I arrived.
And once you look, almost every pattern matches something. A footprint matches a foot. A smooth pebble matches the river that rolled it. Starlight carries the makeup of the star that sent it. Things leave traces of themselves in each other; that’s what it means for them to touch.
So, third try: every pattern is information. The universe, the biggest pattern there is, is information all the way through.





Every pattern
third try: tree rings, starlight
Anything readable
second try: notes, maps
In a mind
first try


Isn’t that circular?
Now there’s a problem. If every pattern is information, what’s a pattern? An arrangement of smaller patterns. In other words, information. I’m using the word to define itself.
Usually that’s the sign of a bad definition. “A dog is a dog” tells you nothing. But not every circular definition is empty.
Here’s one you use every day: a folder is something that holds files and other folders. The word “folder” appears in its own definition, and you still understand folders completely. The definition even tells you the most interesting thing about them: they can sit inside each other as deep as you like. Programmers write functions like this all the time, functions that call themselves. The definition calls itself, and it’s still a complete description of what the function will do.
The difference is that “a dog is a dog” only repeats a word. The folder definition describes how the thing behaves, and the circle is part of the behaviour.
I think information is like that. If it really is the most basic thing there is, there’s nothing more basic to define it with. All you can do is describe how it behaves. (Geometry does the same with points: it never says what a point is, only how points and lines behave, and builds everything from there.) Here’s how information behaves: it’s made of patterns, patterns are made of smaller patterns, and some patterns resemble others. When one resembles another, it tells you something about it.
Where does motion live?
Next problem. Patterns sound still: shapes, arrangements, layouts. But the world moves. Throw a ball and it rises and falls. Where is the information that it’s going to fall?
It isn’t in any single moment. Take a sharp photo of a ball in mid-air and you can’t tell whether it’s on its way up or on its way down. One slice of the world doesn’t hold its motion.
You already know where motion goes, though. Put time along the bottom of a graph and motion turns into a shape. A stock chart is a year of rises and drops drawn as one still line. Plot the ball’s height against time and its whole flight becomes an arc, sitting on the page, complete.


ONE MOMENT






up or down?
ACROSS TIME



time
height



the whole flight: one shape


Physicists take this literally. In Einstein’s relativity, time is a dimension alongside the three of space, and one common way to read it is that the universe is a single four-dimensional shape that never changes. Physicists call this the block universe. The ball’s flight is part of that shape, the same way a slope is part of a mountain. Nothing in the block moves. Motion is what the shape looks like from inside, one slice at a time, like a flipbook: every page is still, and the movement is in the stack.
That also answers where the “must” in “the ball must fall” comes from. A law of physics is a regularity in the shape: every thrown ball, everywhere, traces the same kind of arc.
So once time is part of the picture, the problem goes away. Everything really is information: one enormous pattern, stretched across space and time.
Putting ourselves back in
Now I can go back to the first try, the picture in your head, and see what it was. It wasn’t wrong. It was a special case.
We don’t get to see the shape all at once. We live one slice at a time, always in the present, with no view along time. If you want to know what comes next, the only way is to build a small copy of the pattern that runs faster than the real thing.
A weather forecast does exactly this. A computer runs next week’s weather in a few hours. The copy has the same shape as the real weather, but it lives on a different substrate (chips instead of air) and it’s squeezed into a much shorter time. Because it gets to the end first, it tells you what’s coming. Your head does the same thing when you picture the drive to the airport in a few seconds and decide to leave at six.


THE WORLD · ONE WEEK

THE FORECAST · A FEW HOURS




same peak, but the
copy gets there first


now
time


So the information we care about, the kind the first try called “a picture in a mind”, is this: a small pattern on one substrate, running over a short time, with the same shape as a big pattern running over a long one. The copy finishes before the world does. That’s all a prediction is.
Patterns on patterns
One loose end. I said the copy lives on a different substrate. But a brain is part of the physical world, and so is a computer. Isn’t it all one substrate in the end?
It is, and this is where the circle comes back. A substrate is just a pattern that other patterns can be built on. Think of a video game. Mario runs, jumps and bumps into blocks, and his world has its own rules. You reason about it entirely in those rules. Underneath, it’s code; under the code, a chip; under the chip, electrons. Each layer is a pattern in the layer below, and the ground for the layer above.
Minds work the same way. Ideas sit on neurons, neurons on chemistry, chemistry on physics. We call the top layer the mind, or the world of ideas, because that’s the layer we can reason in. Nobody thinks in neurons. Substrates nest inside each other, just like folders.
Where this lands
Here’s where I’ve ended up. Everything is information: patterns made of smaller patterns, sitting on substrates that are patterns themselves. Some patterns resemble others. When a small, fast pattern resembles a big, slow one, it can tell you how the big one ends. That’s the kind of information living things learned to build, because we’re stuck in the present and have no other way to see what’s coming.
I started with information as something inside me, and ended with me as something inside information. Which raises the next question: if a mind is a small, fast copy of the world, what is the “I” that seems to be doing the copying? That one gets its own article.

Philosophy/What-Is-Logic.title: What Is Logic?
Philosophy/What-Is-Logic.content:
Language, premises, rules, frameworks, and why one contradiction ruins everything

In What Is Information I ended up somewhere simple. Everything is information, and the kind we use is a small, fast pattern that has the same shape as a big, slow one. A weather forecast runs next week in a few hours. Because the copy finishes first, it tells you what’s coming.
With that in place, logic turns out to be much easier to define. If information is the copy, logic is how we run it.
The copy needs somewhere to live
A copy has to be written on something. For most of our thinking, that something is language.
Language does two jobs. It names things: the glass, the table, the floor. And it stores claims about them, of two kinds:

How things are: “the glass is on the edge of the table.”
What follows what: “a glass that falls off a table breaks.”

Put the two together and you can run the world forward without touching it. The glass is at the edge; things at the edge get knocked off; glasses that fall break. Move the glass. Nothing happened in the world. A few words moved around in your head, and they told you how the next ten seconds could go.
Language folds time
Here’s what makes language so good at this. It squeezes time.
Take “it rains every second day.” In the world, that fact is enormous. It’s spread across every day there is, maybe forever. Language turns the repetition itself into a thing, gives it a name, and stores it in one sentence you can carry around.


THE WORLD · DAY AFTER DAY


…



"It rains every second day."


It folds time in a second way too. A line of reasoning keeps its own history. Write out a sum, or think something through, and the earlier steps are still there when you reach the end. Where you started and where you ended up, the present and the future you worked out from it, sit on the same page.
Pictures can do some of this. Plenty of people think visually, and most animals probably think only in pictures. But pictures run out quickly. Try picturing “every second day, forever.” You can say it easily. You can’t really see it.
Premises and axioms: where the copy starts
Every piece of reasoning starts somewhere. In an everyday argument, the starting claims are called premises. “The glass is at the edge” and “glasses that fall break” are premises. When the starting claims define a whole system, like geometry, arithmetic or a game, they’re called axioms. Either way, they do the same job: they’re statements you don’t prove, you just take.
Axioms describe the system. They introduce the parts (the nouns) and how the parts behave (the verbs).
Chess is the cleanest example. The axioms are the rules of the game. There are pieces, a king, a bishop, a knight, and each one moves in a certain way. Nobody proves that a bishop moves diagonally. It’s simply how this system is defined.
Rules: how the copy is allowed to move
You already know how to do the next part. Nobody needs a course to see that “every glass breaks when dropped; this is a glass; so it will break if dropped” works, or that “some glasses are blue; this is a glass; so it’s blue” doesn’t. We all notice when a step doesn’t follow. Formal logic is an attempt to write that instinct down precisely.
The steps are governed by rules of inference. The most famous one (logicians call it modus ponens): if A, and if A then B, then B. The bishop is on this square; if a bishop is on this square, it can reach that one; so it can reach that one.
When the conclusion of an argument follows from its premises like this, the argument is valid. A good rule never takes you from true premises to a false conclusion, whatever they’re about. That’s what logicians actually mean by logic: the study of which steps are safe by their shape alone. “Every dropped glass breaks; this is a glass; so it breaks if dropped” has exactly the same shape as “every cat can fly; Tom is a cat; so Tom can fly”. Both are valid. Whether the conclusion is true depends entirely on the premises. An argument that is valid and starts from true premises is called sound. The flying cat is valid, but not sound.
The rules are a choice too. The standard set is called classical logic, but there are others. Some refuse certain steps the standard set allows, and some are built to tolerate contradictions. Most logicians treat the rules as pure form, known without looking at the world. My own hunch is that the rules we find natural were learned from the world as well: we trust “if A then B” because, over and over, things that followed each other kept following. That’s my view, not the textbook one.
A framework is everything the axioms reach
Start from the axioms and keep applying the rules, and you get a growing tree of consequences: everything that follows. (In mathematics, a consequence someone has actually proved is called a theorem.) Logicians call the whole tree a theory. In everyday English “theory” sounds like a hunch, so I’ll call it a framework, a word philosophers have used in much the same sense.
The odd thing about a framework is that it’s fixed the moment you choose its axioms and rules. Every game of chess that could ever be played is already in the rules. Nobody has played them all, and nobody will. Reasoning doesn’t add anything to a framework; it only uncovers more of what was already there.
Fixed doesn’t mean it answers everything, though. Some frameworks contain questions their own axioms can’t settle either way. Gödel proved that ordinary arithmetic is one of them, which shook mathematics when it came out.
So the question isn’t really when reasoning runs out. It’s how far you can see. A grandmaster and a beginner play inside exactly the same framework. The grandmaster sees ten moves deep, and the beginner sees two.





Axioms
the parts, and how they behave



how far you can see
the framework: everything the axioms reach


Why one contradiction ruins everything
So logic isn’t the framework itself. Logic is the rules for growing it: the steps that never lead from truth to falsehood.
The one thing those rules can’t survive is a contradiction: a claim and its opposite, a copy pointing two ways at once. In standard logic, the damage doesn’t stay local. Once a framework contains a contradiction, you can derive anything from it: the glass breaks, the glass doesn’t break, the moon is made of cheese. Logicians call this explosion. A framework that says everything predicts nothing.
That’s why there’s really only one hard requirement for a set of axioms: they must be consistent, meaning no contradiction can be derived from them. Logicians also like axioms to be independent, meaning none of them can be derived from the others. That keeps things tidy, but nothing breaks if one is redundant.
To falsify a claim is to find it going the other way: it says the glass falls, and the glass doesn’t fall. Close to the ground, that’s easy to see. As the claims get more abstract, you can’t picture them anymore, and that’s exactly where the rules earn their keep. They let you go where your imagination can’t follow. That’s the beauty of abstraction: you can reason your way through systems that feel completely counterintuitive and still land somewhere that predicts.
In everyday thinking, you’re the checker
Here’s the part that’s easy to miss. Ordinary language doesn’t stop you contradicting yourself.
Paper will happily hold “the glass broke” two lines above “the glass didn’t break”. Language stores claims and remembers them. It doesn’t check them. In everyday reasoning, the checking is done by whoever is doing the reasoning: you, a teacher marking your working, or a friend who says “wait, you just said the opposite”.
That’s the whole reason logicians formalised logic. Write the axioms and rules precisely enough, and checking becomes mechanical: a computer can verify a proof line by line without understanding any of it. Everyday thinking never gets that luxury. It runs on loose language and the same instinct that spots a bad step, enforced as best we can, which is why it goes wrong. Usually the rules aren’t the problem. The person checking missed something: a premise stated forty lines back, a step that didn’t quite follow.
Putting it together
Here’s the whole thing in one place, in the words logicians use:

Information is a small, fast pattern with the same shape as a big, slow one.
Language is what we write that pattern on. It names things, stores claims about how they are and what follows what, and folds time into a sentence.
Premises (in an argument) and axioms (in a system) are the starting claims, taken without proof.
Rules of inference are the steps you’re allowed to take, chosen so they never lead from true premises to a false conclusion.
An argument is valid if its conclusion follows from its premises, and sound if it’s valid and its premises are true.
A framework is everything the axioms and rules reach. Logicians call it a theory.
A framework is consistent if no contradiction can be derived in it. One contradiction, and it explodes.
Logic is the study and use of the rules: extending a framework without contradiction, so the copy keeps predicting.

Notice what isn’t in that list: truth. Logic guarantees that each step is safe. Nothing in it checks the premises against the world, and that has consequences, some of them expensive. That’s the subject of Logic Isn’t About Truth.

index.title: Notes
index.content:
I’m Chinmay. This is where I write in public: longer pieces I’m working on, published as they evolve. Some of them are drafts, and they’ll change.
Philosophy
Microframeworks: my working philosophy of how to live. There’s no single “you” in charge of your mind, only small, temporary frameworks taking turns to say “I”. And one question: if you’ll be at peace once you’ve done this thing, why not be at peace first, and then do it?
What Is Information?: starting from the obvious answer (a picture in your head) and fixing it step by step, until information covers everything, including time.
What Is Logic?: built on top of information. Language as the substrate, premises and axioms, rules of inference, frameworks, and why one contradiction ruins everything.
Logic Isn’t About Truth: what it costs to mistake logic for a machine that produces truth: cults, smug atheism, bad arguments, and guilt about being inconsistent.
The Soul Is a Product of Ego: why the usual soul (a light inside the body, one per person, mine) looks like the ego’s handiwork: rubber hands, animals, split brains and the narrator that explains things afterwards. And why I still believe in a soul, spread over everything.
Mind
Heart or Mind Is the Wrong Question: what people actually mean by “my heart told me”, why the heart is just whichever side we admire, and the better question to ask: how deep does the argument go?
The Cost of Needing to Understand Everything: for people who can’t learn anything until they understand it to the core, and blame their memory. How that bottom-up habit works, what it costs, and the shift to trusting abstractions.
The War Between You and Your Mind: why the part of you that plans keeps losing to the part that craves (you were born on a sailboat, and the wind isn’t yours), what helps, and why it might be a game rather than a war.
How You Sabotage Yourself Without Knowing It: three traps the mind sets (the tortured genius, trauma as a badge, and buying certainty), why they pay, and how to step out of them.
What Is Ego?: one word for hurt pride and for what monks try to dissolve. Ego as the I-maker plus a bias in your own favour, and why turning it down costs a few highs and buys back your peace.
AI and Work
Why the Age of Abundance Won’t Feel Like One: AI can end a lot of scarcity, but not wanting. Why a world of plenty won’t feel like plenty, and why that’s a reason not to wait for it to be at peace.
Where the Work Goes: if AI moves scarcity instead of ending it, where does work go? Two spectrums (utility to art, and tech to product to sales) and what to get better at now.
